## Two Values Per Person

- so far one score per person; now two things measured per person
- made-up data: practice hours and test score, eight people
- each row = one person, the two values go together

```{r paired-data}
practice <- tibble(
  hours = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8),
  score = c(48, 55, 51, 62, 58, 70, 65, 71)
)

practice
```

```{r paired-scatter, fig.cap="Each point represents one person. People with more practice hours tend to have higher scores.", fig.alt="Scatterplot of eight paired observations showing a positive, imperfect relationship between practice hours and test scores.", echo=FALSE}
ggplot(practice, aes(x = hours, y = score)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, colour = "#467AAC") +
  labs(x = "Practice time (hours)", y = "Test score") +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r paired-scatter-code, ref.label="paired-scatter", eval=FALSE, webex.hide="Show the plot code"}
```

- point out: upward pattern, but not a straight line
- goal: one number for direction and strength of the linear relationship

## Two Distances From The Mean

- link to variance: subtract the mean; now do it for both variables, multiply the two distances per person
- `mutate()` three columns onto `practice`:
  - `dx`: hours minus mean hours
  - `dy`: score minus mean score
  - `product`: `dx * dy`

```{r correlation-pieces-exercise, eval=FALSE}
mean_x <- my_mean(x)
mean_y <- my_mean(y)

deviations <- practice %>%
  mutate(
    dx = ,
    dy = ,
    product =
  )

deviations
```

`r hide("Show a hint")`
- same `mutate()` pattern as squared distances in Chapter \@ref(equations)
- columns are `hours` and `score`
- `product` can use `dx` and `dy` (mutate can use a column it just made)
`r unhide()`

`r hide("Show one solution")`
```{r correlation-pieces}
mean_x <- my_mean(x)
mean_y <- my_mean(y)

deviations <- practice %>%
  mutate(
    dx = hours - mean_x,
    dy = score - mean_y,
    product = dx * dy
  )

deviations
```
`r unhide()`

- `dx`, `dy` = distance above/below each mean

```{r paired-deviations, fig.cap="Zero on each axis means the corresponding variable's mean. Matching signs give positive products; opposite signs give negative products.", fig.alt="Scatterplot of centred hours and scores with zero reference lines. Points mostly fall in the lower-left and upper-right quadrants.", echo=FALSE}
ggplot(deviations, aes(x = dx, y = dy)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_point(size = 3, colour = "#467AAC") +
  labs(x = "Hours minus mean hours", y = "Score minus mean score") +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r paired-deviations-code, ref.label="paired-deviations", eval=FALSE, webex.hide="Show the plot code"}
```

- look at `product` column:
  - above both means: + times + = positive
  - below both: - times - = positive
  - above one, below other: negative

- quick check: if one person's `dx` is -2 and their `dy` is -3, their product is `r fitb(6)`.

## Covariance

- add products, divide by pairs minus one = sample covariance

$$
s_{xy} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y})}{n-1}
$$

- label terms: $i$ keeps a person's two values together; $n$ = number of pairs; sum adds the products

- into code: as in Chapter \@ref(equations), a function only has vectors `x`, `y`, so use them
- distances given; student multiplies, sums, divides by n - 1

```{r covariance-steps-exercise, eval=FALSE}
dx <- x - my_mean(x)
dy <- y - my_mean(y)
products <-
sum() /
```

`r hide("Show a hint")`
- `products` is `dx * dy`; top is `sum(products)`; $n$ is `length(x)`; brackets round `length(x) - 1`
`r unhide()`

- check: to two decimal places, covariance is `r fitb("18.86")`.

`r hide("Show one solution")`
```{r covariance-steps}
dx <- x - my_mean(x)
dy <- y - my_mean(y)
products <- dx * dy
sum(products) / (length(x) - 1)
```
`r unhide()`

}

my_covariance(x, y)
```

`r hide("Show a hint")`
- `dx`, `dy` use `my_mean()` as above; `products` multiplies; `output` = sum / `length(x) - 1`
`r unhide()`

`r hide("Show one solution")`
```{r my-covariance-solution}
my_covariance <- function(x, y) {
  dx <- x - my_mean(x)
  dy <- y - my_mean(y)
  products <- dx * dy
  output <- sum(products) / (length(x) - 1)
  return(output)
}

my_covariance(x, y)
```
`r unhide()`

## Check It Against `cov()`

- `cov()` = R's sample covariance

```{r my-covariance-check}
c(mine = my_covariance(x, y), R = cov(x, y))
all.equal(my_covariance(x, y), cov(x, y))
```

- second, smaller pair:

```{r my-covariance-check-2}
a <- c(2, 4, 9)
b <- c(3, 1, 8)

c(mine = my_covariance(a, b), R = cov(a, b))
all.equal(my_covariance(a, b), cov(a, b))
```

- note: needs same-length numeric vectors, at least two complete pairs, no NAs; keep rows paired (sorting one breaks pairing)
- interpret: covariance positive, above-mean practice goes with above-mean score on balance

- try: same variable in both inputs

```{r covariance-is-variance}
c(covariance = my_covariance(x, x), variance = my_var(x))
all.equal(my_covariance(x, x), my_var(x))
```

- point out: deviation times itself = squared deviation, so covariance with itself = variance

## Why Standardise?

- covariance depends on units: hours to minutes multiplies every deviation by 60

```{r covariance-units}
c(hours = my_covariance(x, y), minutes = my_covariance(x * 60, y))
```

- same people, covariance 60 times larger
- fix: divide by product of the two SDs

$$
r = \frac{s_{xy}}{s_x s_y}
$$

- = Pearson's correlation coefficient, $r$

`r hide("Show a hint")`

`r unhide()`

`r hide("Show one solution")`
```{r my-correlation-solution}
my_correlation <- function(x, y) {
  covariance <- my_covariance(x, y)
  sd_x <- my_sd(x)
  sd_y <- my_sd(y)
  output <- covariance / (sd_x * sd_y)
  return(output)
}

my_correlation(x, y)
```
`r unhide()`

## Check It Against `cor()`

```{r my-correlation-check}
c(mine = my_correlation(x, y), R = cor(x, y))
all.equal(my_correlation(x, y), cor(x, y))
```

```{r my-correlation-check-2}
c(mine = my_correlation(a, b), R = cor(a, b))
all.equal(my_correlation(a, b), cor(a, b))
```

- hours to minutes again:

```{r correlation-units}
my_correlation(x * 60, y)
```

- r = `r round(my_correlation(x, y), 2)`: strong positive linear association in these eight
- why unchanged: SD of hours also times 60, cancels
- range -1 to 1; ends = perfect straight line, sign = direction; near 0 = little linear association (could still be curved, look at the plot)
- zero SD in either variable: undefined (divide by zero)

- check: changing hours to minutes makes Pearson's correlation `r mcq(c(answer = "stay the same", "60 times larger", "negative"))`.

## Your Turn: Two Predictions

- check with practice data:
  1. adding 10 to every score leaves r unchanged
  2. reversing sign of every score reverses sign of r

```{r correlation-exercise, eval=FALSE}
my_correlation(x, y + 10)
my_correlation(x, -y)
```

- explain each using deviations from the mean

`r hide("Show one solution")`
```{r correlation-solution}
c(plus_10 = my_correlation(x, y + 10), reversed = my_correlation(x, -y))
```
- +10: scores and mean both up 10, deviations unchanged
- times -1: every score deviation flips, so products and covariance flip; SD stays positive
`r unhide()`

## A t-Value Again

- sample r describes our data; can also test null: population r = 0
- independent pairs from bivariate normal: this follows a t-distribution under the null

$$
t = r\sqrt{\frac{n-2}{1-r^2}}, \qquad df = n-2
$$

- $n$ = number of pairs; df = $n-2$ (not $n-1$ as in one-sample t)
- same as residual df in simple regression (intercept + one slope)

`r unhide()`

`r hide("Show one solution")`
```{r my-correlation-t-solution}
my_correlation_t <- function(x, y) {
  r <- my_correlation(x, y)
  n <- length(x)
  output <- r * sqrt((n - 2) / (1 - r^2))
  return(output)
}

my_correlation_t(x, y)
```
`r unhide()`

- note: needs at least three complete pairs and r strictly between -1 and 1; our functions don't check

## Check It Against `cor.test()`

```{r my-correlation-t-result}
correlation_result <- cor.test(x, y, method = "pearson")
correlation_result
```

- `t` should match ours; as with `t.test()` in Chapter \@ref(t-statistic), `$statistic` + `unname()`

```{r my-correlation-t-check}
c(mine = my_correlation_t(x, y), R = unname(correlation_result$statistic))
all.equal(my_correlation_t(x, y), unname(correlation_result$statistic))
```

- match; t = `r round(my_correlation_t(x, y), 2)`, df = `r length(x) - 2`

## Is It Significant?

- `cor.test()` also gives a p-value
- r becomes a t, so the one-sample p-value tools work too; see bonus correlation section in Chapter \@ref(p-values)
- caution: correlation doesn't show practice caused higher scores; made-up data says nothing about real students

## Try It On Real Data

- `sleep` data from Chapter \@ref(standard-error): every patient tried both drugs, so two values per patient
- second-drug rows in same patient order as first, so positions line up
- question: do patients who gain more on one drug gain more on the other?

```{r real-data-ch7}
drug_1 <- sleep %>% filter(group == 1) %>% pull(extra)
drug_2 <- sleep %>% filter(group == 2) %>% pull(extra)
drug_result <- cor.test(drug_1, drug_2)

c(mine = my_correlation(drug_1, drug_2), R = cor(drug_1, drug_2))
all.equal(my_correlation(drug_1, drug_2), cor(drug_1, drug_2))
all.equal(my_correlation_t(drug_1, drug_2), unname(drug_result$statistic))
```

- strongly positive: some patients respond more to both drugs
- comes back in Chapter \@ref(two-sample-t), changes how we compare the drugs

# My statistics functions
#
# Add each function you build to this file, under the heading of the
# chapter you built it in. Later chapters load it with
# source("my_functions.R"), so every function here can be reused.
#
# Keep only the functions in this file. Run and check them in your
# exercise files, not here.
#
# Some functions return a tibble, so load the tidyverse before using them.


# PART I: BUILDING TEST STATISTICS =========================================


# From Equations to Code ---------------------------------------------------
my_mean <- function(x) {
  total <- sum(x)
  n <- length(x)
  output <- total / n
  return(output)
}

my_var <- function(x) {
  n <- length(x)
  mean_x <- my_mean(x)
  squared_distances <- (x - mean_x)^2
  total_squared_distance <- sum(squared_distances)

  output <- total_squared_distance / (n - 1)
  return(output)
}



# Spread and Standard Error ------------------------------------------------
my_sd <- function(x) {
  output <- sqrt(my_var(x))
  return(output)
}

my_se <- function(x) {
  n <- length(x)
  sd_x <- my_sd(x)
  output <- sd_x / sqrt(n)
  return(output)
}

my_summary <- function(x) {
  output <- tibble(
    n = length(x),
    mean = my_mean(x),
    variance = my_var(x),
    sd = my_sd(x),
    se = my_se(x)
  )
  return(output)
}

my_z_score <- function(x) {
  mean_x <- my_mean(x)
  sd_x <- my_sd(x)
  output <- (x - mean_x) / sd_x
  return(output)
}



# The One-Sample t-Test ----------------------------------------------------
my_t_value <- function(x, comparison_value) {
  mean_x <- my_mean(x)
  se_x <- my_se(x)
  output <- (mean_x - comparison_value) / se_x
  return(output)
}

my_t_test <- function(x, comparison_value) {
  t <- my_t_value(x, comparison_value)
  df <- length(x) - 1
  output <- tibble(t = t, df = df)
  return(output)
}



# Covariance and Correlation -----------------------------------------------
my_covariance <- function(x, y) {
  dx <- x - my_mean(x)
  dy <- y - my_mean(y)
  products <- dx * dy
  output <- sum(products) / (length(x) - 1)
  return(output)
}

my_correlation <- function(x, y) {
  covariance <- my_covariance(x, y)
  sd_x <- my_sd(x)
  sd_y <- my_sd(y)
  output <- covariance / (sd_x * sd_y)
  return(output)
}

my_correlation_t <- function(x, y) {
  r <- my_correlation(x, y)
  n <- length(x)
  output <- r * sqrt((n - 2) / (1 - r^2))
  return(output)
}

## Link Back And Next Step

- variance: squared deviations from one mean; covariance: paired deviations from two means
- covariance / two SDs = correlation; correlation to t, so Part II p-value and power tools work for it too
